description: Green AI is a team from Cameroon using AI and NASA Earth data to push the frontier of smart agriculture. We help smallholder farmers in Buea and across Cameroon predict rainfall, detect crop stress, and make better planting decisions — even with low internet and low-cost phones. Our mission: make African agriculture smarter, greener, and climate-resilient.
summary: crop rotation  advisory system for small holder farmers in Buea Cameroon with the use of NASA telemetry and satellite data
details:
YENLU - Buea Slope Watch is a community early-warning web app for landslides and floods in Buea, Cameroon. It shows a live map of five high-risk quarters: Molyko, Great Soppo, Bonduma, Buea Town, and Bokwango, with each quarter coloured Green, Yellow, or Red. It works by pulling rainfall data for Buea from NASA POWER and Open-Meteo, then running it through a simple risk engine inspired by NASA's LHASA model that combines rainfall with slope and MODIS land-cover and vegetation data. If rain is over 60mm in three days the quarter turns Red, 30 to 60mm turns Yellow, and anything less stays Green. Residents can also tap Report Flood / Landslide, pick their quarter, upload a photo and write what happened, and that report appears instantly as a pin on the map for neighbours and local authorities to see.

People in Buea no longer have to wait for radio news after a landslide has already happened. They can see their own quarter's risk before it happens, and they can see real reports from neighbours in real-time. The app is built to work on a phone in low bandwidth, and it uses free open NASA data so a local council can run it for free. It also turns residents from victims into reporters, giving them a way to warn each other directly.

The intended impact is to reduce deaths and blocked roads from landslides and flash floods on the slopes of Mount Fako. In the short term, it gives faster warnings for families in Bonduma, Bokwango and Great Soppo. In the long term, it builds a local database of where floods and landslides actually happen in Buea, so the council can decide where to build drains and retaining walls, and where not to allow building.

The project was built with JavaScript, HTML, CSS and Python, with a JavaScript and Leaflet web map on the frontend, a http://Node.js and Python API on the backend, and PostgreSQL for the database. For DevOps we used Docker and Docker Compose with three containers for frontend, backend and database, plus GitHub and GitHub Actions. The data sources were NASA POWER rainfall, Open-Meteo, NASA MODIS for land cover, NDVI vegetation and land surface temperature, and the NASA LHASA model as inspiration. For hardware we used a laptop and a phone for field photos in Buea.

The project is creative because most early-warning systems are top-down, going from satellite to government to a warning that never reaches the street. YENLU is both bottom-up and top-down. It combines NASA satellite data that people cannot easily read, with phone photos that people can read. A grandmother in Molyko does not need to understand MODIS, she just sees that Bonduma is Red today and that three neighbours posted photos of a blocked road. We also made it Lite on purpose, with no heavy AI and no expensive servers, so it can actually run in Cameroon.

In building it, the team considered low internet, so the app is lite with no heavy satellite images loaded on the phone. We used local knowledge, with real quarters people know instead of GPS coordinates. For trust, reports need a photo and a quarter, not just anonymous text. For safety, we never ask for an exact house location, only quarter level. For cost, we used only free NASA open data with no paid APIs. And for sustainability, Docker makes it runnable with one command.
